tagline: From Zero to Fluent in AI

modules.title: What Even Is AI?
modules.subtitle: Strip away the sci-fi hype and see how modern AI actually works in plain English.

chapters.title: AI vs. Regular Software: Rules vs. Patterns
chapters.summary: Traditional software follows exact instructions written by humans line by line. Modern AI learns fuzzy patterns from millions of examples so it can handle messy real-world tasks like language and images.

analogy.title: The Calculator vs. The Seasoned Chef
analogy.body: A pocket calculator is regular software: press 2 + 2 and it follows rigid electrical rules to return 4 every single time. Modern AI is more like a seasoned chef who has tasted ten thousand dishes. You cannot write a simple math rule for "make this soup taste cozy," yet the chef recognizes patterns in ingredients and improvises a great bowl.

sections.heading: How regular software thinks: strict recipes
sections.body:
Almost every app you used before 2022—spreadsheets, alarm clocks, banking portals, and calculators—was built using explicit rules. A human programmer sat down and wrote out every single scenario in advance: "If the user clicks Save, store the file. If the password is wrong, show a red warning."

This approach is unbeatable whenever the rules are crisp and unchanging. You want your bank balance to follow exact arithmetic, never a creative guess. The trouble starts when humans try to write fixed rules for messy, everyday tasks.

callout.title: Try writing a rigid rule for a cat
callout.body: How would you explain a cat to a computer using only rules? "Four legs, whiskers, pointy ears." Wait—what if the cat is curled up sleeping, hiding one leg, or viewed from behind? Humans spent decades trying to code those rules by hand and still got fooled by fuzzy pillows.

sections.heading: How AI flips the script: learning from examples
sections.body:
Instead of hand-writing a million brittle rules, AI researchers tried something radically different: show a computer millions of labeled examples and let math adjust internal dials until the computer spots the patterns itself.

Those internal dials are called model weights (or parameters). During a huge upfront study phase called training, the system sees billions of sentences, photos, or lines of code, makes guesses, checks how wrong it was, and nudges those weights slightly closer to the right pattern. Once training finishes, the weights are frozen and ready to use—a phase called inference.

callout.title: Myth Buster: AI does not "understand" like a human brain
callout.body: Even when an AI writes a heartfelt poem or explains taxes clearly, there is no conscious person inside the server having feelings or memories. It is applying extraordinarily rich statistical patterns learned during training.

sections.heading: When to use AI—and when regular software wins
sections.body:
Because AI works with probabilities rather than rigid formulas, it shines at drafting emails, summarizing messy notes, translating tone, writing starter code, and brainstorming ideas. At the same time, regular software still beats AI at exact arithmetic, accounting ledgers, and tasks that must behave identically 100% of the time.

The best modern tools combine both worlds: AI handles the messy human request, then hands exact math or file operations off to reliable traditional code.

callout.title: A simple rule of thumb
callout.body: Need exact certainty (like calculating GST on 400 invoices)? Use regular software or a spreadsheet formula. Need judgment on messy text, structure, or creative starting points? Reach for AI.

keyTakeaways: Regular software obeys exact human-written rules; AI learns statistical patterns from vast sets of examples.
Training is the expensive upfront study phase that tunes model weights; inference is the fast everyday act of answering your prompt.
AI excels at messy, open-ended tasks like writing and coding, while regular software still wins at strict, repeatable calculations.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between regular software and modern AI?
options: Regular software runs only on phones, while AI runs only on supercomputers.
Regular software follows exact human-written rules, while AI learns patterns from many examples.
Regular software cannot use the internet, while AI always browses live websites.
Regular software uses math, while AI does not use math at all.
quiz.explanation: Traditional programs execute explicit step-by-step rules coded by programmers. Modern AI learns flexible patterns from massive collections of examples by tuning mathematical weights.

quiz.question: Every time you send a message to ChatGPT or Claude, the AI is permanently retraining its model weights on your chat in real time.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Answering your everyday prompts is called inference—the model weights stay frozen while it generates a reply. Training is a separate, massively expensive process done beforehand.

quiz.question: A friend says: "I need to sum 5,000 exact accounting rows for a tax filing, so I should paste them into an AI chat instead of Excel because AI is smarter." What is the mistake here?
options: AI chats are probabilistic pattern-matchers and can slip on exact arithmetic, whereas a spreadsheet uses rigid rules that are 100% accurate.
Excel cannot open more than 1,000 rows.
AI cannot read numbers at all.
Spreadsheets require an API key to add numbers.
quiz.explanation: Use the right tool for the job! Exact, repeatable arithmetic is where classic software like spreadsheets shines with 100% reliability—save AI for summarizing, categorizing, or writing the formula for you.

chapters.title: What Is an LLM? The World’s Best Pattern-Completer
chapters.summary: A Large Language Model (LLM) generates entire essays, recipes, and programs by doing one deceptively simple job over and over: predicting the single most helpful next piece of text.

analogy.title: Supercharged Autocomplete That Read the Whole Library
analogy.body: You already know autocomplete on your phone keyboard: type "See you at" and it suggests "home" or "work." Now imagine an autocomplete engine that read virtually every public book, textbook, conversation, and code manual on Earth. To accurately guess the next word in a mystery novel or a Python file, it quietly had to learn grammar, logic, history, and coding patterns.

sections.heading: Breaking down the three scary words: L-L-M
sections.body:
Tech news loves acronyms, so let us unpack LLM in ten seconds. "Large" means the model has billions of tuned numbers (weights) and studied an enormous library of text. "Language" means it works primarily with human words and programming languages—though modern versions are also multimodal, meaning they can see images and read PDFs too.

"Model" simply means a mathematical representation of patterns. Put together, a Large Language Model is a giant pattern-matcher built specifically to read and generate language.

callout.title: Why "next-word prediction" turns into real usefulness
callout.body: At first glance, guessing the next word sounds too simple to explain coding or advice. Think about this: to correctly predict the next word after "If a shirt costs $40 with 25% off, the final price is $", the model has to absorb the underlying pattern of percentages!

sections.heading: One piece at a time—not a pre-written script
sections.body:
When you ask an LLM a question, it does not search a giant filing cabinet of pre-written answers. Instead, it writes fresh from scratch, one small chunk (a token) at a time. That is why you literally watch words stream across the screen.

After picking the first token, it feeds that token back in, looks at the whole conversation plus its new word, and predicts the next token—repeating hundreds of times per second until it predicts a special "stop, I am finished" signal.

callout.title: Watching the probability wheel spin
callout.body: If you type "The sun rises in the", the model assigns roughly 99% probability to "east" and tiny fractions to "morning" or "sky". If you type "Write a funny name for a dog:", dozens of options have reasonable probabilities—which is why asking twice gives two creative answers.

sections.heading: How raw predictors become polite assistants
sections.body:
A freshly trained base LLM only knows how to continue internet text—if you ask it "How do I boil an egg?", a raw base model might continue with "How do I fry bacon? How do I make toast?" because that looks like a FAQ list.

To turn it into a helpful assistant, AI labs run a second finishing step (post-training) using human feedback and step-by-step reasoning examples. That teaches the model to answer questions directly, admit uncertainty when appropriate, and follow safety guidelines.

callout.title: Myth Buster: LLMs do not copy-paste web pages from a live database
callout.body: Unless a chat app explicitly gives the AI a web-search tool, an LLM is generating text purely from compressed patterns stored in its frozen weights—not secretly Googling your question in the background.

keyTakeaways: LLM stands for Large Language Model—a giant neural network trained on vast text and code to predict the next piece of text.
LLMs write answers freshly one chunk at a time rather than pulling pre-written replies from a database.
Modern LLMs are often multimodal, meaning they can understand screenshots, photos, and PDFs alongside plain text.

quiz.question: How does an LLM produce a full three-paragraph answer to your question?
options: It copies the top result from a search engine and changes a few words.
It asks five humans in a call center to draft a reply.
It selects one pre-written template stored by human engineers.
It predicts the most likely next chunk of text (token) one step at a time until finished.
quiz.explanation: Every LLM generates replies sequentially through next-token prediction—picking one token, adding it to the text so far, and predicting the next until the response is complete.

quiz.question: Modern multimodal LLMs can accept screenshots or photos in addition to typed text.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! Multimodal models convert images, PDFs, or audio into internal signals alongside text so you can paste a screenshot of an error or design right into the prompt.

quiz.question: Someone says: "I asked an LLM about this morning’s stock price and it got it right, so every LLM clearly has built-in live internet access." Spot the mistake.
options: LLMs cannot read numbers like stock prices.
Stock prices never change during the morning.
A base LLM only knows what was in its frozen training data; live web lookup only happens if the surrounding app gives it a search tool.
Only open-weights models can see stock prices.
quiz.explanation: Raw LLMs have frozen knowledge from training. When an AI knows today’s news or prices, that is because the chat app attached a web-search tool around the model!

chapters.title: Meet the AI Families: Claude, Gemini, GPT & Open-Weights
chapters.summary: Just like car brands offer compact sedans and heavy-duty trucks, AI labs release model families with fast budget options, flagship thinkers, and open-weights models you can run privately.

analogy.title: Airlines and Aircraft Tiers
analogy.body: Calling all AI "ChatGPT" is like calling every smartphone an "iPhone." Today there are several major AI builders—Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), OpenAI (GPT), plus open-weights builders like Meta (Llama) and DeepSeek. Each family offers smaller zippy models for quick errands and flagship models for complex work.

sections.heading: The major closed (hosted) model families
sections.body:
Three major labs lead hosted cloud AI—meaning the models live on the company’s giant servers and you talk to them via a chat app or API:

• **Claude (by Anthropic)**: Beloved for crisp, natural writing, careful instruction-following, and standout coding tools like Claude Code.
• **Gemini (by Google)**: Known for huge context windows (reading massive documents or videos at once), strong multimodal skills, and fast, low-cost Flash models.
• **GPT (by OpenAI)**: The family that kicked off the ChatGPT wave, offering versatile general assistants and deep reasoning models.

callout.title: Notice the three sizes inside almost every family
callout.body: Most labs ship a "Small/Fast" tier (cheap, instant replies for simple tasks), a "Balanced/Workhorse" tier (best everyday quality-to-price), and a "Flagship/Reasoning" tier (slower and pricier, built for thorny planning or tricky bugs).

sections.heading: Open-weights models: Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen & Mistral
sections.body:
Not all powerful AI is locked behind one company’s servers. Open-weights models publish their finished weight files publicly. Anyone—researchers, startups, or curious beginners—can inspect how they behave, rent cheap servers to host them, or even run smaller versions right on a personal laptop with zero internet connection.

Meta’s **Llama**, **DeepSeek**, **Qwen**, and **Mistral** have narrowed the gap with proprietary giants dramatically, driving AI costs down for everyone.

callout.title: Why a normal person cares about open-weights
callout.body: Imagine summarizing private medical receipts or personal journal entries on an airplane with Wi-Fi turned off. An open-weights model running locally on your computer keeps 100% of that text on your own machine—and costs $0 per message.

sections.heading: How to pick a model without overthinking it
sections.body:
Beginners often get paralyzed by version numbers and benchmark charts. You do not need to memorize scores! In practice, the difference between good models matters far less than giving clear instructions.

Start with one fast, generous workhorse model for everyday questions, reach for a stronger coding/reasoning tier when designing an app or untangling a stubborn bug, and explore local open-weights models whenever you want free offline practice.

callout.title: Myth Buster: Bigger and more expensive is not always better
callout.body: Using the most expensive flagship model to format a grocery list is like renting a cargo plane to pick up milk. Smaller models like Gemini Flash or GPT mini respond in a split second at a tiny fraction of the cost.

keyTakeaways: Major AI model families include Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), GPT (OpenAI), and open-weights models like Llama and DeepSeek.
Most families come in speed/cost tiers: fast & cheap models for quick jobs, balanced models for daily work, and flagship models for hard reasoning.
Open-weights models publish their trained weight files publicly so you can host them cheaply or run them privately on your own computer.

quiz.question: What makes an "open-weights" model like Llama or DeepSeek different from a closed cloud-only model?
options: Open-weights models can only write short one-sentence answers.
Their trained weight files are published publicly so people can host or run them on their own hardware.
They never use tokens.
They require a $200/month subscription to download.
quiz.explanation: Open-weights means the trained parameter files are shared publicly. That lets individuals and businesses run them privately on local machines or third-party servers.

quiz.question: You should always pick the largest, most expensive flagship AI model for every simple task like fixing spelling in an email.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Fast, smaller tiers handle everyday proofreading, summarizing, and quick formatting in a split second for a tiny fraction of the cost.

quiz.question: A coworker says: "ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all just different websites connected to the exact same single AI brain." What is wrong with that claim?
options: They are separate model families built and trained independently by different companies (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) with different strengths.
Claude is not available on websites.
Gemini only works on Android phones.
OpenAI owns Anthropic and Google.
quiz.explanation: GPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), and Gemini (Google) are distinct model families trained separately by different teams—each with its own writing style, context limits, and pricing.

chapters.title: Chat Apps vs. Raw Models: What’s Really Under the Hood
chapters.summary: When you open ChatGPT, Claude.ai, or Gemini in a browser, you are not talking straight to a bare model—you are using a polished app packed with memory, hidden instructions, and extra tools.

analogy.title: The Car Engine vs. The Full Dealership Car
analogy.body: A raw AI model is like a V6 engine sitting on a wooden crate. By itself it has huge power, yet you cannot drive it to the grocery store. A chat app like Claude.ai or ChatGPT bolts on the seats, dashboard, GPS, fuel gauge, and cupholders so any driver can hop in and go.

sections.heading: What a raw AI model actually does by itself
sections.body:
Strip away the colorful website and a raw model is shockingly minimalist. You send it a chunk of text (and maybe an image), and it sends back a chunk of text. That is it!

A raw model has no saved sidebar of past chats, no "Upload PDF" button, no built-in internet search, no memory of who you were yesterday, and no way to edit files on your computer. Every single request starts with a completely blank slate unless software sends the prior messages back in.

callout.title: Why raw models feel like they have amnesia
callout.body: Raw models are stateless—they do not remember your previous message on their own! Every time you send message #5 in a chat app, the app quietly re-sends messages #1, #2, #3, #4, AND #5 together behind the scenes.

sections.heading: All the invisible extras a chat app adds for you
sections.body:
When you type into ChatGPT, Claude.ai, or Gemini, the chat wrapper quietly performs half a dozen helpful tricks before and after calling the model:

• **Chat history & memory**: Saves past conversations in a sidebar and re-sends recent turns automatically.
• **Hidden system instructions**: Tells the model today’s date, how to format tables cleanly, and when to stay safe.
• **Built-in tools**: Decides when to search the web, run Python code for math, read uploaded PDFs, or render a live webpage preview.
• **Friendly interface**: Streams words smoothly, highlights code blocks, and offers one-click copy buttons.

callout.title: Same model, wildly different experience
callout.body: If you ask a raw model via API "What is the weather in Mumbai right now?", it says it cannot check live weather. Ask the exact same model inside a chat app with web search enabled, and it silently searches Google and hands you the forecast in two seconds.

sections.heading: Why knowing this distinction unlocks superpowers
sections.body:
Once you see the seam between the **raw model** and the **app wrapped around it**, the entire AI ecosystem stops looking mysterious. Coding tools like Claude Code, browser assistants, and apps you build yourself are all simply new wrappers plugging into the exact same raw models—just wired to different tools like your project folder or a spreadsheet.

In the upcoming modules, you will learn how text turns into tokens, how API credits pay for raw model calls, and how developer tools called harnesses give models hands to build real software.

callout.title: Preview of Module 4
callout.body: When a wrapper is specifically engineered to give an AI file access, terminal commands, and multi-step loops, builders call it an AI Harness. You will explore that hands-on in Module 4!

keyTakeaways: A raw AI model only takes text/media in and returns text out—it has no built-in chat history, web browser, or file access.
Chat apps like ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and Gemini are wrappers that add history, hidden instructions, file uploads, and web search around a raw model.
Understanding the split between raw models and wrapper apps explains how coding tools, agents, and custom AI apps work.

quiz.question: Why does a chat app appear to remember message #1 when you send message #5?
options: The raw model permanently memorizes every user’s face and name.
Models can only have five-message conversations.
Your Wi-Fi router stores the AI’s memory.
The chat app quietly bundles and re-sends earlier messages from the conversation along with message #5.
quiz.explanation: Raw models are stateless! The chat app saves your history and quietly sends the earlier messages back to the model each time you hit Send.

quiz.question: A raw AI model by itself already includes a chat sidebar, PDF upload button, and live web search without any wrapper app.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! A raw model simply takes input and generates output. Sidebars, PDF readers, and live web search are all features added by the chat app or harness built around the model.

quiz.question: Priya asks a raw API model to check today’s cricket score and gets "I do not have access to real-time data." She concludes: "The API uses a dumber model than the website!" Spot her mistake.
options: The API cannot answer sports questions.
APIs only run on Sundays.
It can be the exact same model—the website simply wrapped it with a live web-search tool that the raw API call did not attach.
Websites never use LLMs.
quiz.explanation: Same brain, different accessories! The consumer chat site adds web search and other tools automatically, while a plain API call talks directly to the bare model unless you attach tools.

modules.title: Tokens, Context & Talking to AI
modules.subtitle: Learn how AI slices your text, why it forgets long chats, and how to prompt cleanly.

chapters.title: What Are Tokens? Why AI Reads Chunks, Not Letters
chapters.summary: AI does not read English letter by letter or even strictly word by word. Before a model sees your message, a tokenizer chops it into bite-sized numbered pieces called tokens.

analogy.title: Lego Bricks of Language
analogy.body: Imagine building sentences out of Lego bricks instead of individual letters. Common everyday words like "house" or "coffee" come as a single pre-molded brick. Less common words like "unbelievable" snap together from three smaller bricks: "un" + "believ" + "able". Every AI model reads, counts, and charges by the brick.

sections.heading: Why AI uses tokens instead of letters or whole words
sections.body:
Computers only understand numbers, so every piece of text has to be turned into numbers before an AI can process it. If we numbered every single letter (a=1, b=2), sentences would turn into super long chains that are slow to read. If we numbered every possible word in every language plus typos and code names, the dictionary would explode to millions of entries.

Tokens are the sweet spot in the middle. A program called a tokenizer keeps a vocabulary of roughly 50,000 to 200,000 common word pieces. In everyday English, **1 token equals roughly ¾ of a word**—so 100 tokens is about 75 words, and a 300-word email is around 400 tokens.

callout.title: Why AI sometimes miscounts the "r"s in "strawberry"
callout.body: Because the tokenizer hands the model chunks like ["str", "aw", "berry"] represented as ID numbers—not individual spelled-out letters—counting letters inside a chunk feels like counting how many bricks are inside a sealed box without opening it!

sections.heading: Spaces, emojis, code, and other languages cost different tokens
sections.body:
Not all characters cost the same number of tokens. Punctuation, blank spaces, and leading spaces often attach right onto the start of a word token. Meanwhile, emojis, complex code symbols, and non-English scripts (like Hindi, Tamil, Arabic, or Japanese) frequently split into 2 to 4 tokens per word or symbol.

That means two messages that look the same length on screen can use very different token counts under the hood.

callout.title: Try it yourself in the Token Playground
callout.body: Head into the Token & Context Playground lab after this chapter and type your own name, an emoji like 🚀, and a sentence in another language—you will see the colored token bricks light up instantly!

sections.heading: Three everyday reasons tokens matter to you
sections.body:
You never need to count tokens manually, yet knowing they exist immediately clears up three common mysteries:

1. **Speed**: Generating 1,000 tokens takes roughly twice as long as generating 500 tokens because the model creates one token at a time.
2. **Memory limits**: Every AI has a maximum token budget per conversation (its context window).
3. **Cost**: When you use pay-as-you-go API credits in Module 3, providers bill per million tokens—not per message or per minute.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "One token = one word"
callout.body: Close, but not exact! Short common words like "cat" are 1 token, long words like "extraordinary" are 2–3 tokens, and messy URLs or emojis can burn through tokens surprisingly fast.

keyTakeaways: A token is a chunk of text (roughly ¾ of an English word) that AI models read, generate, and measure.
A tokenizer converts your text into numbered tokens going in and converts the model’s numbered tokens back into readable words coming out.
Tokens explain why AI occasionally struggles with spelling puzzles, why longer replies take longer, and how AI pricing works.

quiz.question: Roughly how many English words equal 100 tokens?
options: About 10 words
About 1,000 words
About 75 words
Exactly 100 letters
quiz.explanation: In typical English text, 1 token is roughly ¾ of a word—so 100 tokens works out to around 75 words.

quiz.question: An emoji or a word in a non-English language can sometimes use more than one token.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! Tokenizers optimize common English words into single tokens, while emojis, special symbols, and less-frequent scripts often split into 2–4 tokens.

quiz.question: Sam thinks: "My AI miscounted the letters in strawberry, which proves it is bad at all logic and coding." What is the real explanation?
options: The AI does not know the English alphabet.
The tokenizer feeds the AI whole word-chunks as numbers rather than individual characters, making letter-counting awkward even for strong reasoning models.
Strawberry is a copyrighted word blocked by AI.
AI can only count up to two.
quiz.explanation: Letter-counting quirks come from how tokenizers chunk text into multi-letter pieces before the model even sees them—not from an inability to reason.

chapters.title: The Context Window: AI’s Working Desk
chapters.summary: Every AI model has a fixed "working desk" called its context window. Understanding how that desk fills up explains why super long chats get sluggish, pricey, or forgetful—and how to keep them sharp.

analogy.title: Papers on a Working Desk
analogy.body: Picture an analyst sitting at a desk of fixed size. Every instruction you give, every PDF you attach, every back-and-forth message, and every reply the AI writes is another sheet of paper spread across that desk. Once the desk is covered edge to edge, sliding a brand-new sheet onto the front pushes the oldest sheet off the back—out of sight and completely forgotten.

sections.heading: What actually sits inside the context window?
sections.body:
Beginners often think the context window only counts the single message they just typed. In reality, it holds **everything** active in that conversation at once:

• Hidden system instructions and tool descriptions
• Files, screenshots, or code snippets you attached
• Every previous message you sent in this thread
• Every previous reply the AI generated
• The new answer the AI is about to write right now

callout.title: How big are modern context windows?
callout.body: Early AI models had tiny 4,000-token desks (about 6 pages). Today’s models commonly offer 128,000 to 200,000 tokens (a thick 400-page book), and some Gemini models stretch up to 1,000,000+ tokens!

sections.heading: Why a cluttered desk still hurts quality
sections.body:
Even if your model boasts a massive 200,000-token desk, piling 80 unrelated topics onto one endless chat thread causes "context rot." Just like a human trying to focus at a messy desk buried in old receipts, the AI can get distracted by dead-end ideas or outdated code you abandoned twenty messages ago.

Even worse, because the app re-sends the whole desk on every turn, a bloated chat gets slower and uses far more tokens on every single message.

callout.title: Start a fresh chat when switching topics
callout.body: Finished planning your weekend trip and now want help writing a resume? Click "New Chat"! A clean desk gives faster, smarter, and cheaper answers.

sections.heading: Keeping long projects crisp without losing your work
sections.body:
What if you are working on one big project—like designing a website—and your chat gets really long? You have two pro moves:

1. **Summarize and restart**: Ask the AI, "Summarize all our agreed decisions and current progress in 8 bullet points," copy that crisp summary, and paste it into a brand-new chat.
2. **Use `/compact`**: Modern AI coding tools like Claude Code include a built-in `/compact` command that tidies up the desk for you automatically.

callout.title: Watch out for silent forgetting
callout.body: When a conversation overflows the context window, the AI usually will not shout "I forgot message #1!" It quietly stops seeing the earliest messages—so if it suddenly ignores a rule you set an hour ago, your desk is probably full.

keyTakeaways: The context window is the maximum total tokens an AI can keep on its working desk at once (instructions + files + full chat history + new reply).
Once the context window fills up, older messages get dropped or summarized, causing the AI to forget earlier details.
Starting fresh chats for new topics—or summarizing progress into a clean thread—keeps AI sharper, faster, and cheaper.

quiz.question: Which items count toward a model’s context window on turn 10 of a conversation?
options: System instructions, uploaded files, messages #1–#10, earlier AI replies, and the new reply.
Only the single sentence you just typed in message #10.
Only the AI’s replies, never your prompts.
Only PDFs, never plain text.
quiz.explanation: Everything on the desk counts together: hidden instructions, attached files, all prior back-and-forth turns, and the reply currently being generated.

quiz.question: Keeping one giant 300-message chat thread for every unrelated question all month is the best way to get sharp answers.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Unrelated old messages clutter the context window, distract the model, slow responses down, and burn extra tokens. Open a fresh chat for new topics!

quiz.question: Maya uploaded 40 pages of notes and chatted for two hours. Suddenly the AI ignores a formatting rule she gave in message #1. She thinks: "The AI is stubbornly disobeying me on purpose!" What likely happened?
options: The AI got tired and went offline.
She forgot to capitalize her sentences.
AI models always ignore message #1.
Her long conversation cluttered or pushed message #1 out of the active context window—starting a fresh chat with a short summary will fix it immediately.
quiz.explanation: Long threads dilute or push out early rules. Summarizing your key decisions into a clean new thread (or running `/compact` in CLI tools) restores laser focus.

chapters.title: System Prompts, User Prompts & Temperature
chapters.summary: Great results come less from "secret magic prompts" and more from clear roles, concrete context, and knowing how the creativity dial (temperature) shapes replies.

analogy.title: The Director’s Brief vs. The Scene Line
analogy.body: Imagine filming a movie. The System Prompt is the director’s overall brief handed to the actor before cameras roll ("You play a calm, empathetic family doctor who speaks in simple everyday words"). The User Prompt is the specific line the patient says in that scene ("My knee clicks when I climb stairs"). Temperature is how much improvisation the director allows.

sections.heading: System prompt vs. User prompt: two layers of instruction
sections.body:
Almost every AI conversation has two distinct layers:

• **System Prompt**: Top-level standing rules that set the AI’s persona, tone, format, and boundaries for the entire session. In apps you build (or tools like Claude Code), you write this once so the AI remembers your style automatically.
• **User Prompt**: The specific request you type right now ("Draft a polite 3-sentence reply declining this meeting").

Separating standing rules from today’s task prevents you from repeating "keep it concise and jargon-free" twenty times a day.

callout.title: Vague prompt vs. Clear 4-part prompt
callout.body:
Vague: "Write an email about our workshop."
Clear: "Write a warm 120-word invite email (Goal) for non-technical small-business owners (Audience) announcing our free Saturday AI Basics workshop at 10 AM (Context). End with one bold RSVP link placeholder and no cheesy exclamation marks (Constraints)."

sections.heading: The 4 ingredients of a rock-solid prompt
sections.body:
You do not need to buy "500 secret prompt templates." Nearly every strong prompt simply answers four human questions:

1. **Goal**: What exact outcome do you want?
2. **Context / Audience**: Who is this for, and what background facts matter?
3. **Examples**: Show one sample of the tone or structure you love ("Match this style: ...").
4. **Constraints**: Word limit, format (bullet list, table, JSON), and what to avoid.

Bonus trick: if you are unsure what details matter, finish your prompt with **"Ask me 3 quick clarifying questions before you start."**

callout.title: Show, do not just tell
callout.body: Giving even ONE short example of what "good" looks like beats two paragraphs of abstract adjectives like "make it engaging, punchy, and modern."

sections.heading: Temperature: the predictability vs. creativity dial
sections.body:
Remember how an LLM assigns probabilities to every possible next token? **Temperature** is a numeric dial (commonly `0.0` to `1.0`) that decides whether the model sticks strictly to the top-ranked token or occasionally picks surprising runners-up.

• **Low temperature (0.0–0.2)**: Calm, steady, repeatable. Ideal for extracting invoice numbers, translating accurately, or editing code.
• **Medium temperature (0.4–0.7)**: Natural everyday conversation and clear explanations.
• **High temperature (0.8–1.0+)**: Playful, unexpected, diverse—great for brainstorming brand names or story twists (though too high turns into gibberish!).

callout.title: Myth Buster: Lowering temperature to 0 eliminates hallucinations
callout.body: Temperature 0 makes the AI pick its most predictable guess every time—which makes answers repeatable, NOT guaranteed true. If the model does not know a fact, its most predictable guess can still be confidently wrong!

keyTakeaways: System prompts set standing rules, role, and tone for a whole session; user prompts ask for today’s specific task.
Clear prompts cover four simple pieces: Goal, Context/Audience, Examples, and Constraints—no magic phrases required.
Temperature controls randomness: keep it low for precise, repeatable work and higher for creative brainstorming.

quiz.question: When should you prefer a LOW temperature setting (like 0.0–0.2)?
options: Brainstorming 30 wacky names for a comic book villain.
Writing surreal poetry.
Extracting dates and totals accurately from customer receipts or fixing a software bug.
Making the AI write longer essays.
quiz.explanation: Low temperature keeps the AI steady and focused on the highest-probability tokens, which is ideal for structured extraction, math steps, and reliable code edits.

quiz.question: Setting temperature to 0 guarantees that an AI will never hallucinate or make factual mistakes.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Temperature 0 only makes output more consistent and predictable. If the AI lacks real facts, it can still repeat a plausible-sounding wrong guess.

quiz.question: Alex wants a landing page headline for his neighborhood bakery and types only: "Give me marketing copy." Why will the result feel generic?
options: AI cannot write bakery headlines.
The prompt gave no audience, brand vibe, example, or length constraint—so the model falls back on generic average internet phrasing.
He forgot to say "please".
Marketing copy requires temperature 5.0.
quiz.explanation: Vague inputs produce average generic outputs. Adding who the bakery serves, the vibe (cozy sourdough vs. luxury pastry), and a short length constraint transforms the result immediately.

chapters.title: Hallucinations: Why AI Sounds Confident When It’s Wrong
chapters.summary: AI does not lie out of malice—it invents plausible-sounding falsehoods because predicting smooth text is its core job. Learn the simple verification habits that keep you completely safe.

analogy.title: The Smooth Improv Actor
analogy.body: Think of an AI like a brilliantly eloquent improv actor on stage. If someone shouts "Tell us about the 1842 Treaty of Bluebell!", the actor refuses to freeze in silence—they smoothly invent an ambassador’s name, a cozy town, and a realistic clause that fits the rhythm of a history book. It sounds 100% confident even though none of it happened.

sections.heading: Why hallucinations happen in the first place
sections.body:
Because an LLM generates words by asking "What token looks most likely to come next?", its training rewards fluent, helpful-sounding answers. When you ask about something rare, hyper-specific, or brand new—like an obscure book citation, a small local restaurant’s hours, or a software feature released yesterday—the model may not have exact facts stored in its weights.

Instead of stopping cold, it fills the blank with whatever looks statistically right: a realistic author name, a plausible URL, or a convincing phone number. Researchers call this a **hallucination**.

callout.title: High-risk spots where AI hallucinates most
callout.body: Always double-check: exact legal/medical claims, academic citations and page numbers, live prices or store hours, exact quotes, and obscure biographical dates.

sections.heading: Grounding: turning a closed-book guess into an open-book check
sections.body:
The single best antidote to hallucinations is **grounding**—putting the real source material right onto the AI’s desk instead of asking it to recall from memory.

Rather than asking "What is my company’s refund policy?", paste the actual refund policy text into the prompt and ask: *"Using ONLY the policy pasted below, answer the customer’s question and quote the exact sentence. If the policy does not say, reply: Not covered in the document."* Giving the AI explicit permission to say "I do not know" cuts guesswork dramatically.

callout.title: The "Quote the source" prompt pattern
callout.body: Add this line whenever summarizing important PDFs, contracts, or articles: "Only use facts explicitly stated in the text above. Cite the exact heading or line for every claim, and flag anything missing."

sections.heading: A 30-second verification checklist for everyday life
sections.body:
You do not need to be paranoid about AI—just treat it like a sharp, fast intern whose work you glance over before signing your name:

1. **Check high-stakes facts at the source**: Click links, open the official site, or check the original document for numbers, dates, and medical/legal advice.
2. **Verify code by running it**: Never assume code works because it looks neat—run it and click the buttons! (We will practice this in Modules 6 and 7.)
3. **Ask AI to critique itself**: Prompting "List any assumptions you made or places where you might be uncertain" often catches shaky spots right away.

callout.title: Safe mental model
callout.body: Trust AI for drafts, structure, explanations, and starting points. Verify AI for facts, numbers, links, and final decisions.

keyTakeaways: A hallucination is a fluent, confident-sounding invention produced because LLMs optimize for plausible text patterns.
Grounding—pasting source documents or enabling live web search—turns risky memory guesses into verifiable open-book answers.
Give AI explicit permission to say "I don’t know," and always verify high-stakes facts, quotes, links, and code before relying on them.

quiz.question: What is the most effective way to prevent hallucinations when asking AI questions about your own apartment lease?
options: Paste the lease text into the prompt (grounding) and tell the AI to answer strictly from that text and quote the exact clause.
Ask the AI to promise it will not lie.
Type the question in ALL CAPS.
Raise the temperature to 1.0.
quiz.explanation: Grounding places the exact source document on the AI’s working desk so it reads and quotes real clauses instead of guessing generic lease terms from memory.

quiz.question: If an AI writes a detailed citation with an author name, journal title, and publication year, that guarantees the paper actually exists.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Citations are one of the most famous places LLMs hallucinate—they know exactly what a realistic citation looks like and can assemble convincing fake ones unless verified.

quiz.question: Jordan asks an AI (without web search): "What time does the new cafe on Oak Street close tonight?" and drives over based on its confident "9:00 PM" reply. What went wrong?
options: AI cannot read street names.
Cafes never close at 9:00 PM.
Oak Street is too short of a prompt.
Without live web search or grounded info, the AI guessed a plausible cafe closing time from general patterns instead of checking real hours.
quiz.explanation: Local live facts like business hours are classic hallucination territory when ungrounded. Always check live sources (or a search-grounded tool) for current real-world details.

modules.title: AI Credits, Pricing & API Keys
modules.subtitle: Demystify subscriptions vs. pay-as-you-go credits, API keys, safety rules, and free local AI.

chapters.title: Chat Subscriptions vs. Pay-As-You-Go AI Credits
chapters.summary: Paying $20/month for ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro is completely separate from buying API credits. Learn which billing model fits your habits so you never overpay or get surprised.

analogy.title: The All-You-Can-Eat Buffet vs. The Prepaid Coffee Card
analogy.body: A monthly chat subscription (like ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, or Gemini Advanced) is an all-you-can-eat buffet: pay one flat fee per month and eat inside the restaurant whenever you want (with fair-use pauses if you sprint too fast). Pay-as-you-go AI credits are a prepaid coffee card: load $5, take the coffee anywhere—including into your own apps and coding tools—and pay exact pennies only for the tokens you actually consume.

sections.heading: Why two separate billing systems exist
sections.body:
One of the #1 confusions for beginners happens right here: *"I already pay $20/month for Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus—why is this developer console asking me to add $5 of credits?"*

Consumer chat apps and developer APIs are billed separately at almost every AI company. Your $20/month subscription covers chatting inside their polished website and mobile app (plus some select desktop/CLI bundles depending on your plan). Meanwhile, **AI Credits** pay for raw programmatic access through their API—the pipe that lets outside tools, automations, and apps you build talk directly to the model.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Using the API is expensive and only for big tech companies"
callout.body: Surprise: for light or medium builders, pay-as-you-go API credits are often MUCH cheaper than a $20/month subscription! Five dollars of credits on a fast model can easily fund hundreds—even thousands—of chats and small projects.

sections.heading: When a subscription wins vs. when AI credits win
sections.body:
Choose a **monthly chat subscription** when:
• You chat casually every day in the browser or phone app.
• You want zero setup, built-in web search, voice mode, and predictable flat monthly pricing.

Choose **pay-as-you-go AI credits** when:
• You use AI sporadically (say, three weekends a month) and do not want a recurring $20 bill.
• You want to plug AI into your own websites, apps, spreadsheets, or tools like Marain.
• You want freedom to swap between Gemini, Claude, and GPT inside one tool.

callout.title: Start with a $5 prepaid test balance + hard cap
callout.body: Most providers let you load $5 prepaid credits with auto-reload turned OFF. That way, even if you experiment all month, your maximum possible spend is literally $5—zero surprise bills.

sections.heading: Watch out for "wrapped" credit markup in third-party apps
sections.body: Many trendy AI websites charge you $29/month for "500 AI credits" that secretly call the exact same Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI APIs costing them $1 behind the scenes. That convenience can be fine if the tool saves you hours, yet once you know what raw API credits cost—and how BYOK ("Bring Your Own Key") apps work—you can choose intentionally instead of paying mystery markups.

callout.title: Real-world cost perspective
callout.body: Sending a 500-word question and receiving a 500-word answer uses roughly 1,400 total tokens. On a fast model like Gemini Flash or GPT-4o mini, that entire back-and-forth costs less than $0.0005—about one twentieth of a single US cent!

keyTakeaways: Monthly chat subscriptions (flat fee inside the provider’s own app) and pay-as-you-go API credits (metered per token for external apps/tools) are billed separately.
Prepaid AI credits let light users and builders pay exact fractions of a cent per prompt instead of $20 every month.
Turning off auto-reload and setting a $5 spending cap eliminates any risk of surprise bills while learning.

quiz.question: How do pay-as-you-go AI credits typically bill you?
options: A fixed $50 fee every time you open your laptop.
Only if you build a mobile app.
By how many minutes you keep your browser tab open.
Based strictly on the number of input and output tokens your requests actually use.
quiz.explanation: API credits are metered directly by token count (typically quoted per million tokens), so idle time costs $0 and short prompts cost tiny fractions of a cent.

quiz.question: Paying $20/month for a consumer chat website automatically includes unlimited free API credits for external apps you build.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Consumer web/mobile chat subscriptions and developer API credit balances are separate billing systems at major AI providers.

quiz.question: Rohan wants to try building a small personal tool on weekends, so he skips API credits because he assumes they cost at least $100/month. What did he misunderstand?
options: Weekend API usage is banned.
API credits only work on Windows.
He can load as little as $5 of prepaid credits with auto-reload off—often lasting months for light personal building.
You have to pay $100/month to get a password.
quiz.explanation: Prepaid API credits have no mandatory monthly fee! A small $5 balance with auto-reload off is one of the safest, cheapest ways for beginners to experiment.

chapters.title: What Is an API & an API Key? (The Waiter and the Pass)
chapters.summary: An API is just a clean digital menu for software to talk to software, and an API key is the secret badge proving your account is allowed to place orders.

analogy.title: The Restaurant Waiter and Your VIP Tab Card
analogy.body: Imagine dining at a restaurant. You (your app) do not wander straight into the blazing kitchen (the AI server farm). Instead, you hand a clear order slip to the waiter (the API), who walks it to the kitchen and carries your finished meal back to the table. Your API key is the secret card linked to your tab—the waiter checks it so the kitchen knows whose account to bill.

sections.heading: What actually happens during an AI API call
sections.body:
The acronym **API** (Application Programming Interface) sounds intimidating, yet it is simply a predictable URL on the internet that accepts a neatly formatted text package (usually JSON) and returns a neatly formatted answer.

Whenever a BYOK app—like Marain or a website you create—sends a prompt to Claude, Gemini, or OpenAI, three tiny things travel over an encrypted `https://` connection:

1. **The destination URL** (which AI kitchen to call)
2. **The header with your API key** (proving who is ordering)
3. **The message body** (which model you want, your system prompt, and your message)

A second or two later, the server sends back the reply text plus exact token counts.

callout.title: Peeking at a real API payload in plain English
callout.body: Under the hood, an API call literally looks like a tidy grocery list: `{ "model": "claude-sonnet", "prompt": "Explain photosynthesis in 2 sentences" }`. You can inspect one live in the API Keys & Credits Lab!

sections.heading: What an API key looks like—and what BYOK means
sections.body:
When you sign up on Google AI Studio, Anthropic Console, or OpenAI Platform and click **"Create API Key,"** the site generates a long random string like `sk-ant-api03-8xK9...` or `AIzaSy...`.

Many modern desktop tools offer **BYOK (Bring Your Own Key)**. Instead of charging you a steep subscription markup, the app stays free or one-time purchase, and you optionally plug in your own API key so your computer talks straight to your chosen AI provider at wholesale token prices.

callout.title: Copy it once, store it neatly
callout.body: For security, most providers show your brand-new API key ONLY ONCE the moment you create it. Paste it right into your password manager or local app settings—and if you ever lose it, simply delete the old key and mint a fresh one in 5 seconds.

sections.heading: You can create, label, and revoke keys anytime
sections.body:
Good news for anxious beginners: an API key is NOT permanent like your Social Security number! You can create separate labeled keys for each project (for example, `marain-learning` and `weekend-recipe-app`).

If you ever stop using an app or suspect a key leaked, one click on **Revoke / Delete** shuts that key off instantly worldwide without touching your main account.

callout.title: Treat every API key like a live credit card
callout.body: Anyone who obtains your key can run thousands of AI requests on your dime within seconds. Never paste a real key into group chats, YouTube comments, screenshots, or public code files!

keyTakeaways: An API is a structured digital waiter that lets one app send prompts to an AI provider and receive structured replies back.
An API key is a long secret string (`sk-...`) that identifies your account and links usage to your credit balance.
You can generate separate keys per app and revoke any key in one click if you ever stop using it or suspect a leak.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of an API key when calling an AI provider?
options: It makes the AI model smarter and increases its context window.
It proves who you are and links the API request to your billing/credit account.
It converts English into tokens.
It unlocks offline mode without internet.
quiz.explanation: Your API key authenticates your request—just like a linked payment badge—so the provider knows which account is authorized and which credit balance to charge.

quiz.question: If you accidentally share an API key in a screenshot, you have to delete your entire account because API keys can never be revoked.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! You can revoke (delete) a single compromised API key in seconds from your provider’s dashboard and immediately generate a fresh replacement.

quiz.question: In a help forum, Jamie asks why his code is broken and pastes his full request including `Authorization: Bearer sk-proj-9482a...`. What critical mistake did Jamie make?
options: He posted his live secret API key publicly where bots can scrape and drain his credits within minutes.
He used Bearer instead of Basic.
API requests cannot be discussed on forums.
He forgot to include his home address.
quiz.explanation: Automated bots constantly scan public forums and GitHub for strings starting with `sk-` or `AIza`. Always replace your key with `YOUR_API_KEY_HERE` before sharing snippets or screenshots!

chapters.title: Keeping API Keys Safe: `.env` Files & Never Leaking Secrets
chapters.summary: You do not need to be a cybersecurity expert to keep API keys bulletproof. Learn the three tiny golden rules—`.env`, `.gitignore`, and spending caps—that protect every pro builder.

analogy.title: The Locked Safe Next to Your Public Blueprints
analogy.body: Imagine sharing the architectural blueprints of your dream house online so friends can admire the layout. You would NEVER draw your front-door alarm PIN directly onto the blueprint! Instead, the blueprints stay shareable while your alarm PIN sits in a private note taped inside your wallet. In software, your code is the blueprint and your `.env` file is the private wallet note.

sections.heading: Golden Rule #1: Never hardcode secrets in your code files
sections.body:
The #1 beginner mistake when building with AI is pasting an API key straight into `script.js` or `index.html`, like `const apiKey = "sk-ant-12345..."`.

There are two huge dangers here. First, if you ever share that folder or upload it to GitHub, your key goes public forever in version history. Second, **anything inside a public website’s HTML or JavaScript can be viewed by every visitor** with one right-click ("Inspect Source"). Front-end website code is like writing on a billboard—never put a secret on a billboard!

callout.title: The 60-second bot sweep
callout.body: Security researchers have tested pushing a fake API key to a public GitHub repo—automated scraper bots often discover and try to abuse leaked keys in under 60 seconds. If a key ever leaks, revoke it immediately first, then clean up.

sections.heading: Golden Rule #2: Use a `.env` file paired with `.gitignore`
sections.body:
Professionals separate secrets from code using two tiny plain-text files sitting in the project folder:

• **`.env`**: Stores your private keys locally on your computer (`OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...`). Your local program reads the key from this file automatically.
• **`.gitignore`**: Lists file names that Git must NEVER upload to GitHub. Putting `.env` inside `.gitignore` guarantees your secrets stay safely on your laptop while your clean code gets backed up.

Pro habit: create a harmless template file named `.env.example` containing `OPENAI_API_KEY=paste-your-key-here` so anyone (including future you) remembers what key name the project expects.

callout.title: What a safe project folder looks like
callout.body:
Inside `.env` (private, ignored by Git): `GEMINI_API_KEY=AIzaSyRealSecret123`
Inside `.gitignore` (committed): `.env`
Inside your server code: `process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY` — zero secrets in sight!

sections.heading: Golden Rule #3: Set a hard spending cap & keep keys off public frontends
sections.body:
Even pros make typos, so always add a financial seatbelt: go to your provider’s Billing -> Usage Limits screen and set a hard monthly budget (such as **$5 or $10**) plus an email alert at 50%.

And remember: if you ever build a public website where strangers click an "Ask AI" button, your secret API key must live on a small backend server (or let visitors enter their own key in local settings), never baked into the webpage’s browser files.

callout.title: Ask your AI coding tool to double-check!
callout.body: Before publishing any project, ask your AI assistant: "Scan my folder and verify that no API keys are hardcoded and that .env is listed in .gitignore."

keyTakeaways: Never hardcode an API key directly inside HTML, client-side JavaScript, screenshots, or files uploaded to GitHub.
Store secrets in a local `.env` file and add `.env` to `.gitignore` so Git never uploads your keys.
Always configure a hard monthly spending cap ($5–$10) in your provider dashboard as an automatic safety net.

quiz.question: Why do builders put `.env` inside their `.gitignore` file?
options: To make the website load faster on mobile phones.
To compress images automatically.
To turn off dark mode.
To prevent Git from accidentally uploading private API keys stored in `.env` to GitHub.
quiz.explanation: `.gitignore` tells Git to skip listed files completely—keeping your `.env` secrets strictly on your local computer while safely syncing your code.

quiz.question: Putting your secret API key inside a public website’s `script.js` file is safe as long as you do not display it visually on the page.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Any visitor’s browser downloads `script.js` in full—anyone can open Developer Tools ("Inspect") and read your secret key in two seconds.

quiz.question: Neha notices she accidentally pushed her real `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` to a public GitHub repository two minutes ago. She deletes the line in a new commit and thinks: "Phew, now it is completely safe!" What is her mistake?
options: GitHub does not allow deleting lines.
Anthropic keys automatically change every minute anyway.
Old Git commits stay visible in history and bots may already have copied the key—she MUST revoke/rotate the leaked key immediately in Anthropic’s dashboard.
She just needs to rename `.env` to `.txt`.
quiz.explanation: Once a key touches a public repo or screenshot, assume it is compromised forever. Revoke it in the provider dashboard right away and generate a brand-new key!

chapters.title: Reading Token Pricing & Free Local Models Like Ollama
chapters.summary: AI pricing tables look cryptic until you learn one simple trick: reading "per 1M tokens" and distinguishing input vs. output costs. Plus, discover how to run real AI on your own computer for $0.

analogy.title: Wholesale Rice Pricing vs. Growing Herbs on Your Windowsill
analogy.body: Seeing "$3 per million tokens" is like seeing a grocery wholesaler quote "$10 per metric ton of rice." You are not buying a whole ton for dinner—your single bowl costs less than a penny! And running a local model like Ollama is like keeping a basil pot on your windowsill: once you set it up, every leaf you pick is completely free and offline.

sections.heading: How to read an AI pricing table in 15 seconds
sections.body:
Open any provider’s pricing page and you will see two numbers per model—for example, **$0.30 / 1M input tokens** and **$1.20 / 1M output tokens**.

• **Input tokens** are everything you send to the model (system prompt, chat history, pasted documents).
• **Output tokens** are the fresh words the model generates back. Output tokens typically cost 3× to 5× more because generating each new token requires heavier computation than reading input in parallel.

Quick mental math: divide any "per 1M" price by **1,000** to get the cost per 1,000 tokens (~750 words). So $3 per 1M tokens equals just **$0.003** (three tenths of a cent!) per 750 words.

callout.title: How far does $5 actually go?
callout.body: At ~$0.15/1M input and ~$0.60/1M output (typical budget fast-model rates), a 1,000-token question + 500-token reply costs ~$0.00045. Five dollars buys roughly **11,000 conversations**! Even on a mid-tier flagship model (~$3 input / $15 output), $5 still covers hundreds of rich coding chats.

sections.heading: Three quiet ways bills grow faster than expected
sections.body:
Because per-call prices are tiny, beginners usually spend pennies—except in three sneaky situations:

1. **Huge repeating chats**: Re-sending a 50-page PDF on every single back-and-forth turn multiplies input tokens fast (though modern "prompt caching" discounts repeated inputs).
2. **Runaway loops**: An automated script that calls an AI in an infinite loop by mistake—which is why your $5 spending cap is magic.
3. **Using flagship reasoning models for tiny tasks**: Use fast models for simple summaries and save heavy thinkers for hard problems.

callout.title: Test numbers in the API Credits Calculator
callout.body: In the API Keys & Credits Lab, slide prompt length and messages per day across Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, GPT-4o mini, and Ollama to develop an instant gut feel for real costs.

sections.heading: Free & Private: running local models with Ollama
sections.body:
What if you want zero cloud bills, zero API keys, and 100% privacy? Tools like **Ollama** make running open-weights models on your own Linux, Mac, or Windows machine ridiculously simple.

After installing Ollama, one tiny terminal command—like `ollama run llama3.2` or `ollama run qwen2.5`—downloads a compact model right onto your drive. From then on, it runs completely offline for $0! Smaller 3B–8B parameter models run smoothly on everyday laptops with 8–16 GB RAM, while larger models appreciate a dedicated graphics card (GPU).

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Local models need a $10,000 server"
callout.body: Huge 400B frontier models do need big servers, but modern compact models (3B–14B parameters) run right on ordinary consumer laptops and are shockingly capable for offline notes, practice, and coding help!

keyTakeaways: Divide a provider’s "per 1M tokens" rate by 1,000 to see the tiny cost per ~750 words—and remember output tokens cost more than input tokens.
Watch out for endlessly long repeating threads and unguarded loops; keep chats tidy and enable hard billing caps.
Ollama lets you download and run open-weights AI models directly on your own computer for $0 with full offline privacy.

quiz.question: Why are output tokens almost always priced higher than input tokens?
options: Providers charge extra for punctuation.
Generating brand-new output tokens one by one requires much more compute per token than reading input text.
Input tokens are always free.
Output tokens are translated into multiple languages first.
quiz.explanation: Reading your prompt happens in fast parallel batches, while writing each output token sequentially takes more work—so providers usually price output 3× to 5× higher than input.

quiz.question: Running a local open-weights model through Ollama requires paying per-token API fees to OpenAI.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Ollama runs downloaded open-weights models directly on your own computer’s hardware—no cloud API key, no per-token bill, and it even works offline.

quiz.question: Tariq sees a model priced at "$1.00 per 1M input tokens" and closes the tab thinking "I cannot afford $1 every time I send a message!" What did he misread?
options: 1M means one MILLION tokens (~750,000 words)—a typical 500-word message costs less than a tenth of a single cent!
1M means one message.
The price is per year.
Input tokens are only charged to businesses.
quiz.explanation: 1M = 1,000,000 tokens (roughly ten full novels!). A normal short message costs around $0.0007 at $1/1M—less than a tenth of a cent.

modules.title: AI Harnesses, Tools & Agents
modules.subtitle: Understand the leap from text-only chatbots to AI agents that read files, use tools, and ship real work.

chapters.title: Model vs. Harness: The Engine and the Car
chapters.summary: Why does the exact same AI model feel mediocre in one app and magical in another? The secret is the AI Harness—the software body wrapped around the model.

analogy.title: Same Engine, Completely Different Vehicles
analogy.body: Put the exact same powerful engine inside a bare go-kart with no headlights or steering wheel, and you barely leave the driveway. Put that exact same engine inside a finely tuned rally car with GPS, brakes, suspension, and a dashboard, and you conquer mountain roads. In AI, the LLM is the engine and the AI Harness is the car.

sections.heading: What an AI Harness actually does
sections.body:
You have probably heard builders argue about Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or Antigravity—even when those tools all call the exact same underlying Claude, Gemini, or GPT models! Why do they feel so different?

Because an **AI Harness** is the complete orchestration program wrapped around the raw model. It controls:

• **What context enters the desk**: Automatically loading the right project files and instructions.
• **Which tools exist**: Wiring up file reading, editing, terminal commands, or browser previews.
• **How steps repeat**: Running the model in a loop until tests actually pass.
• **Safety guardrails**: Pausing for your approval before running risky actions and keeping context trimmed.

callout.title: Raw model vs. Harnessed agent on one task
callout.body: Ask a raw chatbot: "Fix the broken signup button in my project." It can only reply with guesses like "Try checking line 20 of your HTML." Ask the exact same model inside a coding harness: it opens your real files, spots the exact typo on line 47, edits it, runs the test suite, and confirms the button works!

sections.heading: Why great harnesses matter just as much as smarter models
sections.body:
Imagine hiring a world-class architect—then locking them in a dark room with no measuring tape, no blueprints, and no phone. Even a genius cannot remodel your kitchen from inside a locked closet!

A well-built harness unlocks the room: it hands the model accurate blueprints (your files), a tape measure (tests and terminal checks), and clean safety locks so it cannot knock down a load-bearing wall without asking you first.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Claude Code is a completely different LLM than Claude"
callout.body: Claude Code is a **harness** (specifically a command-line agent harness) powered by Claude models. The magic comes from combining a strong model with great file tools, clear diff reviews, and smart context management.

sections.heading: What makes a beginner-friendly harness
sections.body:
When evaluating any AI tool, look past flashy demos and check four practical harness traits:

1. **Transparency**: Does it show you which files it read and what lines it wants to change?
2. **Approval controls**: Can you say Yes or No before edits or commands run?
3. **Context hygiene**: Does it help keep long sessions tidy (like `/compact`)?
4. **Easy undo**: Does it work smoothly with Git or checkpoints so mistakes take one second to reverse?

callout.title: Experience it side by side
callout.body: In the Harness & Agent Simulator lab, you can run the exact same bug-fix mission first with a Raw Model (zero tools) and then with Harness capabilities toggled on—you will immediately see the Engine vs. Car difference.

keyTakeaways: The LLM is the engine; the AI Harness is the surrounding software (context loading, tools, execution loop, and safety controls) that turns raw intelligence into real action.
The exact same model can behave dramatically better inside a thoughtful harness than inside a plain text box.
Good harnesses give you clear visibility, approval prompts before changes, and safe undo.

quiz.question: In the "Engine vs. Car" analogy, what role does the AI Harness play?
options: The complete surrounding vehicle—tools, context manager, execution loop, and safety brakes—that lets the raw model get real work done.
The fuel bill you pay every month.
The training dataset used years ago.
Your internet router.
quiz.explanation: The LLM is the engine; the AI harness provides the steering, tools, context management, and safety checks that let the engine actually inspect files and finish tasks.

quiz.question: Two different AI coding apps using the exact same underlying model can produce very different results depending on the quality of their harness.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! How a harness selects files, formats tool outputs, runs verification tests, and manages the context window makes a massive difference in real-world reliability.

quiz.question: Ben pastes "Fix my website’s broken navigation menu" into a plain web chatbot without sharing any files, and gets frustrated when the AI cannot edit his laptop directly. What is he missing?
options: He forgot to upgrade his Wi-Fi speed.
AI models are legally blocked from editing HTML.
Websites cannot have navigation menus.
A plain web chatbot has no local file-editing harness—he either needs to paste the files in or use a local harness like Claude Code CLI that has tools to inspect and edit his folder.
quiz.explanation: A raw chat box in your browser is sandboxed away from your local hard drive. To read and patch project files directly, the model needs a harness equipped with file tools!

chapters.title: Tool Calling & MCP: The "USB-C" for AI
chapters.summary: A language model only outputs text—so how on earth does it read files, check calendars, or search databases? Meet Tool Calling and MCP (Model Context Protocol), the universal plug connecting AI to your world.

analogy.title: A Brain Passing Request Slips + USB-C Plugs
analogy.body: Imagine a brilliant strategist sitting behind a glass wall. They cannot touch a keyboard directly, so they write a structured request slip: "TOOL: read_file, PATH: menu.html" and slide it under the glass. The harness reads the slip, fetches the file, and slides the contents back! MCP is like standardizing all those tools onto USB-C so one universal cable plugs into any AI app.

sections.heading: How tool calling works behind the curtain
sections.body:
Even inside the fanciest agent, an LLM still NEVER directly clicks your mouse or edits your hard drive. Instead, the harness sends the model a menu of available tools in its system prompt—such as `read_file`, `edit_file`, `search_web`, or `run_tests`.

When the model realizes it needs fresh information, it pauses normal chat and emits a structured **tool call** (a tiny JSON slip like `{"tool": "read_file", "path": "index.html"}`). The harness catches that slip, checks permissions, executes the real tool, and hands the exact result back to the model as the next message!

callout.title: A three-second tool call in action
callout.body:
1. You ask: "How many rows are in sales.csv?"
2. Model emits tool call: `read_file("sales.csv")`
3. Harness reads the real file from disk and returns 142 rows.
4. Model counts accurately (or runs a tiny script) and answers: "There are 142 rows—zero guessing!"

sections.heading: The old cable mess—and why MCP was invented
sections.body:
Before 2024, connecting AI to external tools was a nightmare. If you built a Slack integration for ChatGPT, it would not work in Claude or VS Code—every single app needed its own custom glue code. It was like the old days when every Nokia, Sony, and camera needed a completely different charger.

**MCP (Model Context Protocol)** solved this with one open standard: **"USB-C for AI."** Build an MCP server once for Notion, Google Drive, GitHub, Figma, or a database, and ANY MCP-compatible AI harness can plug straight into it in seconds.

callout.title: Two halves of an MCP plug
callout.body: Your AI app (like Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or an IDE) is the **MCP Host/Client**. Each tool connector (like a GitHub or Google Calendar plugin) is a tiny **MCP Server**. Plug them together and your AI immediately learns new capabilities.

sections.heading: Staying safe when connecting tools
sections.body:
Connecting AI to real tools is exhilarating—and deserves common-sense guardrails. Give tools the **minimum permissions** they need: start with read-only access (reading calendar or files) before granting write/send access (sending emails or deleting files).

Also keep your eyes open for untrusted text from the internet: never let an agent automatically run purchases, send emails to strangers, or delete folders without your explicit human approval.

callout.title: Read-only vs. Write actions
callout.body: Reading a file or searching docs is harmless. Editing files, sending Slack messages, or running terminal commands changes the real world—keep approval prompts ON for write actions until you trust the workflow!

keyTakeaways: Tool calling lets an LLM output a structured request slip asking its harness to read files, search the web, or run commands and return real results.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is "USB-C for AI"—one universal open standard letting any AI harness connect cleanly to external tools and data.
Start with read-only permissions and keep human approval enabled for actions that edit, delete, or send messages.

quiz.question: Why is MCP (Model Context Protocol) often nicknamed "USB-C for AI"?
options: It charges your laptop faster while chatting with AI.
It only works with physical USB cables.
It provides one open universal standard so any compatible AI app can plug into external tools and data sources without custom one-off connectors.
It replaces the need for an LLM.
quiz.explanation: Just like USB-C ended the drawer full of mismatched chargers, MCP gives every AI harness and tool provider one shared way to connect cleanly.

quiz.question: During tool calling, the raw AI model secretly bypasses the harness and edits files directly on your computer without the harness knowing.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! The model only outputs a structured text request asking for a tool. The harness receives that request, enforces your permissions/approvals, runs the tool, and sends the result back.

quiz.question: On day one, Sam connects his AI assistant to his work email MCP server and sets "Auto-approve sending emails without asking me." What risk did he overlook?
options: MCP does not support email.
Giving auto-approve write/send permission lets a single misunderstood instruction or hallucination fire off real emails to coworkers before Sam can review them.
Email requires open-weights models.
Auto-approve uses 100× more tokens.
quiz.explanation: Always separate read-only convenience from real-world write actions! Let AI draft emails freely, and keep a human-in-the-loop "Approve Send" button turned on.

chapters.title: How AI Agents Loop: Think, Act, Observe, Approve
chapters.summary: A regular chatbot speaks once and stops. An AI agent runs in a self-correcting loop—thinking, using a tool, checking real feedback, pausing for your approval, and repeating until the job actually works.

analogy.title: Assembling a Bookshelf One Check at a Time
analogy.body: Nobody builds a bookshelf with their eyes closed in one motion. You look at the manual (Think), tighten two screws (Act), give the shelf a gentle wiggle to see if it holds straight (Observe), and tighten a loose bolt before moving on. An AI agent works the exact same way—checking real feedback after every step instead of guessing blindly.

sections.heading: Single-shot chat vs. the multi-step Agent Loop
sections.body:
In a traditional one-turn chat, you ask a question and the AI takes a single blind swing. If its first draft of code has a tiny typo, the chat just ends and leaves you stuck.

An **AI Agent** wraps the model in a repeating loop:

1. **Think**: Break the goal into the next concrete step.
2. **Act**: Call a tool (read a file, edit CSS, run a test).
3. **Observe**: Read the real output—did the test pass, or did an error appear?
4. **Repeat (or Finish)**: If an error popped up, adjust the plan and try again; once checks pass, present a clear summary to you!

callout.title: Watching an agent fix a real bug in 4 beats
callout.body:
Goal: "Make the newsletter form validate emails."
• Loop 1: Reads `form.js` to see existing code.
• Loop 2: Adds email validation + asks you to approve the diff.
• Loop 3: Runs tests—spots a typo on line 18 in the error output!
• Loop 4: Fixes line 18, re-runs tests -> All green -> Reports Done!

sections.heading: Human-in-the-Loop: you stay the pilot
sections.body:
People sometimes picture "AI Agents" as runaway robots doing mysterious things while you sleep. In everyday beginner building, the best agents are **collaborative co-pilots** with built-in **Human-in-the-Loop** checkpoints.

Whenever the agent wants to edit a file, install software, or run a shell command, it pauses and shows you exactly what it plans to do. You click **Approve** (or say *"Wait, keep the button blue instead"*). You never lose control of your project.

callout.title: Give the agent a way to verify its own work
callout.body: Agents get 10× smarter the moment they can **observe** reality! Telling an agent "Run the test command after editing" or "Check the live preview" lets it catch and fix its own tiny slips automatically.

sections.heading: When agents get stuck—and how to unstick them in 10 seconds
sections.body:
Occasionally an agent falls into a spin: trying the same broken fix three times in a row. As the human pilot, spotting a loop is easy—just press Stop (or `Esc` / `Ctrl+C`) and nudge it out:

• Ask it to step back: *"Pause editing. Explain in 3 plain sentences why this error keeps happening."*
• Shrink the step: break a huge request into one tiny verifiable piece.
• Clear cluttered context if the thread has been spinning for a long time.

callout.title: Never leave an unguarded agent looping forever
callout.body: Every loop step sends the conversation back to the model—which consumes tokens! Always supervise agents on new tasks, set billing caps, and interrupt early if you see it repeating itself.

keyTakeaways: An AI agent runs a repeating Think -> Act -> Observe loop so it can inspect real results and fix mistakes instead of guessing once.
Human-in-the-Loop checkpoints keep you in the driver’s seat, letting you approve edits and steer direction at every key step.
If an agent repeats a failing step twice, pause it, ask for a plain-English diagnosis, or break the goal into a smaller step.

quiz.question: What is the correct repeating sequence of a standard AI Agent Loop?
options: Think -> Act (call a tool) -> Observe (read real output) -> Adjust or Finish
Guess -> Delete -> Reboot
Train -> Publish -> Forget
Ask once -> Never check if it worked
quiz.explanation: The power of an agent comes from observing real feedback (file contents, error logs, test results) after each action and adapting until the goal is verified.

quiz.question: Using an AI agent means you must let it make unlimited changes automatically without ever reviewing or approving its actions.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Human-in-the-Loop approvals are a core feature of safe AI harnesses—you stay in charge and approve file edits or commands as you go.

quiz.question: An agent tries the exact same broken command four times in a row while building Leo’s app. Leo walks away for lunch hoping attempt #25 works. What should Leo have done instead?
options: Bought a faster mouse.
Deleted the entire project.
Raised the temperature to 2.0.
Stopped the loop right away (saving tokens), asked the agent to diagnose the root cause in plain English, or narrowed the task to one smaller step.
quiz.explanation: An agent stuck repeating a failed step burns tokens without making progress. Interrupt early, ask for a plain-English diagnosis, and give it a cleaner clue or smaller step!

chapters.title: Instruction Files (`CLAUDE.md`), Rules & Skills
chapters.summary: Tired of repeating your project preferences every time you start a new chat? Learn how plain-English instruction files like `CLAUDE.md`, rules, and reusable skills give your AI permanent house manners.

analogy.title: The Fridge Note vs. The Recipe Card Box
analogy.body: Imagine hiring a helpful house-sitter. Taped right on the fridge is a short welcome note (`CLAUDE.md` / Rules): "Lock the back porch, feed the cat half a scoop, never touch the breaker box." Tucked in a drawer is a recipe card box (Skills): they only pull out the "How to Restart the Wi-Fi Router" card on the rare day the internet drops.

sections.heading: What is `CLAUDE.md` (or `AGENTS.md`)?
sections.body:
Because every fresh AI session starts with a clean desk, repeating *"This is a beginner site using plain HTML and CSS, please keep design warm and minimal, and always explain changes simply"* gets old fast.
